metadata.title: Unraveling the nexus: Culture, cognitive competence, and economic performance across 86 nations (2000–2018)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is cross-national and uses country-level aggregates derived from official PISA reports (means, spans, and tilts) rather than student microdata. Because the analysis is conducted at the country level (N=86 countries with at least one PISA participation between 2000 and 2018), standard PISA student sampling weights and replicate weights are not applicable in the way they would be for student-level ILSA analyses. The authors do not report applying any complex-survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and instead treat the extracted country factor scores as manifest inputs for subsequent regression and path analyses. The main preprocessing steps are construction of PISA-derived variables (5th–95th percentile spans; math–reading tilts) and factor-score extraction for latent constructs (Factor Score Regression), plus handling of missingness in the World Value Survey item set via item exclusion rules.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent variables in the empirical models are country-level PISA-derived factor scores (means, spans, and tilts) computed from published PISA results, not student-level PV-based achievement scores. The paper does not describe a PV-based missing-data procedure (e.g., PV-specific imputation or pooling) because it does not analyze student microdata with PVs. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported in a PV sense for the ILSA component; instead, missingness is addressed in the World Value Survey item construction via exclusion criteria for items/countries with insufficient data coverage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Cross-national dataset restricted to countries with at least one PISA participation between 2000 and 2018, yielding 86 countries for which PISA-derived variables (general factor scores for means across seven waves and competencies; general factor scores for spans computed from 5th–95th percentile differences; and math–reading tilts) were extracted. PISA 2022 was excluded due to COVID-19 concerns. For the Axiological Cube, World Value Survey items were selected across waves 4, 5, 6, and 7; items with insufficient cross-wave data were excluded (e.g., one item excluded due to inconsistent measurement across waves; additional items excluded when no data were found in any wave; and items removed when country coverage fell below a threshold of Nctry < 65), and longitudinal mean values were computed after rejecting longitudinal factor-score extraction.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 (country-level means; math/reading/science; general factor across waves)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (N=86 countries): culture-only R2—AXC=0.627, REL=0.404, HCD=0.256. With controls (Model B): AXC R2=0.536; with economic controls (Model C): AXC R2=0.452. Standardized effects (examples): AXC1 Religiosity & Authority β=-0.78* (Model A), β=-0.63* (Model B), β=-0.55* (Model C); REL2 Protestants β=0.27* (Model A) and β=0.22* (Model B); REL3 Muslims β=-0.46* (Model A), β=-0.27* (Model B), β=-0.25* (Model C); REL4 Three Teachings β=0.24* (Model A), β=0.29* (Model B), β=0.23* (Model C).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 country-level means the study leveraged Axiological Cube dimensions (especially Religiosity & Authority) and religious affiliation shares (Muslims; Three Teachings) to predict PISA means, finding that Religiosity & Authority and Muslims share were strongly negatively associated with cognitive competence while Three Teachings and (weakly) Protestants were positively associated. This indicates that culture-related constructs—particularly those capturing religiosity/authority and specific religious traditions—may be more informative for cross-national competence differences than broad Hofstede-style dimensions, though the analysis is correlational and does not establish causal mechanisms.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 (country-level spans; 5th–95th percentile differences; general factor across waves/competencies)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (N=86 countries): culture-only R2—AXC=0.323, REL=0.133, HCD=0.235 (reported as R2 for spans models). With controls (Model B): AXC R2=0.234; with economic controls (Model C): AXC R2=0.226. Standardized effects (examples): AXC2 Sexual Traditionalism β=0.57* (Model A), β=0.63* (Model B), β=0.49* (Model C); AXC1 Religiosity & Authority β=0.04 (Model A), β=-0.29 (Model B), β=-0.05 (Model C); REL3 Muslims β=0.37* (Model A), β=0.16 (Model B), β=0.53* (Model C); HCD2 Long-term Orientation & Restraint β=0.26* (Model A), β=0.25* (Model B), β=0.23* (Model C).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 country-level span the study leveraged Axiological Cube dimensions and religious affiliation shares to predict educational inequality (spans), finding that Sexual Traditionalism was the most consistent positive predictor of larger gaps between low and high performers while Religiosity & Authority showed little or inconsistent association. This indicates that some culture-linked value systems may align with greater within-country inequality in achievement, suggesting that equity-oriented policy may need to consider cultural context rather than relying solely on average performance targets.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 (country-level tilts; math-reading difference; factor score tilt)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression (N=86 countries): culture-only R2—AXC=0.212, REL=0.137, HCD=0.132. With controls (Model B): AXC R2=0.109; with economic controls (Model C): AXC R2=0.061. Standardized effects (examples): AXC1 Religiosity & Authority β=-0.44* (Model A), β=-0.65* (Model B), β=-0.56* (Model C); AXC2 Sexual Traditionalism β=0.67* (Model A), β=0.28 (Model B), β=0.18 (Model C); REL1 Catholics β=-0.25 (Model A), β=0.05 (Model B), β=0.16 (Model C); HCD4 Uncertainty Avoidance β=-0.19 (Model A), β=-0.14 (Model B), β=-0.16 (Model C). Path analysis (controlled model B): direct effect of PISA tilt on economic growth βDir.=0.272.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 country-level tilt the study leveraged Axiological Cube and religious affiliation variables to predict STEM orientation (math–reading), finding that Religiosity & Authority was consistently negatively associated with tilts and that culture explained substantially less variance in tilts once controls were added. This indicates that cultural factors may be better aligned with explaining overall competence and inequality than with explaining relative STEM orientation, implying that STEM-focused educational policy may require mechanisms beyond broad cultural value dimensions.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2018 (country-level means/spans/tilts as mediators; economic growth outcome)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Path analyses (N=86 countries): controlled model B shows direct effect of PISA tilt on economic growth βDir.=0.272. Indirect effects (examples, controlled model B): Three Teachings via PISA means—indirect effect AB=0.152* with R2=0.540; Power Distance & Collectivism via PISA means—indirect effect AB=-0.153* with R2=0.544; Religiosity & Authority via PISA means—indirect effect AB=-0.244* with R2=0.404; Sexual Traditionalism via PISA means—indirect effect AB=-0.309* with R2=0.594. For PISA spans as mediator: Long-term Orientation & Restraint indirect effect AB=0.027 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2018 country-level competence indicators as mediators for economic growth, the study found that PISA tilt had a positive direct association with economic growth (βDir.=0.272) and that several cultural dimensions influenced growth primarily indirectly through PISA means rather than through direct effects. This indicates that improving national student competence (as captured by PISA means) may be a key pathway linking cultural value systems to economic performance, though the study remains correlational and cannot confirm causal mediation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes cross-national relationships between national culture and student competence using PISA country-level results from 2000–2018 (seven waves) and constructs three PISA-derived outcomes: means (general factor across waves/competencies), spans (general factor of 5th–95th percentile differences), and tilts (math–reading difference). The authors do not use student-level PVs or ML prediction; instead, they apply Factor Score Regression with multiple regression and path analyses across 86 countries (PISA 2022 excluded). Culture measured via religious affiliations, Hofstede’s 6-D model (recoded to four dimensions), and an Axiological Cube (from World Value Survey items) explains substantial variance in PISA means (e.g., AXC culture-only R2=0.627) and smaller variance in spans and tilts, with Religiosity & Authority showing strong negative associations. In controlled path models, PISA tilt has a positive direct effect on economic growth (βDir.=0.272), while cultural effects largely operate indirectly through PISA means. Limitations include correlational design, country-level aggregation, and no survey-weight/PV-based uncertainty quantification at the student level.
